To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the efficiency of sampling of ground-dwelling beetles and ants in pitfall traps depends on the habitat type and the intensity of sampling effort.

(1) pitfall trap sampling of ground beetles in NW Patagonia was highly efficient, as it captured a high proportion (90%) of the total number (n = 60) of known species, (2) pitfall trap samples of ground beetles did not capture a high proportion of species (n = 10) that are known to be present in the area, and (3) pitfall trap capture efficiency was higher in burned than in unburned habitats.
the species richness of ground-dwelling beetles and ants in the study region was high and showed some concordance, but also idiosyncrasy in response to habitat type and disturbance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a rapid species diversity assessment for the study of the effect of habitat disturbance on species richness patterns.
the efficiency of a species richness assay of beetles and ant species, in a region of NW Patagonia (Argentina).

the efficiency of a species richness assessment of ground beetles (Coleoptera) and ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae), captured in pitfall trap in natural and disturbed habitats of the Nahuel Hupai Region (NW Patagnoia, Argentina).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of pitfall traps is a useful and efficient method to estimate the species richness of ground-dwelling arthropods in the Nahuel-Huapi National Park.
the efficiency of our rapid species richness assay for ground beetles and ant is high, but that it is not possible to extrapolate the patterns of species richness of beetles to that of ants.

, for a rapid assessment of species diversity of beetles and ant in the Nahuel-Huapi region, a sample-based approach of 19 sites with 342 pitfall-traps is efficient and sufficient to capture most species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rapid assessment protocol used here is a useful tool for monitoring species diversity in a region with a high level of habitat heterogeneity.

a combination of the two groups of insects may be used as an indicator of species diversity patterns, and that the sampling design we propose is a good starting point for a rapid assessment of the biodiversity of ground beetles or ants at the regional level.

, for a rapid and cost-effective assessment of species richness patterns of ground beetles in the NahuelHuapi National Park, the use of pitfall traps at an intensity of one trap/100 m2 in 19 sites would be adequate for the analysis of regional species diversity patterns.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of a rapid species-richness assay of beetles and/or ants may provide an efficient and cost-effective tool for the assessment of biodiversity in natural habitats and those altered by human activity.

a sampling design with a high number of traps, spread in groups, and with two collection stations per sampling unit is efficient to capture the majority of ground beetle and ant species known in the study area.
the sampling effort used in our study is sufficient for the estimation of regional diversity patterns of ground beetles in the study area.
